lead: A model that scores 95% on the data it learned from may fail tomorrow. Cross-validation estimates error on unseen data by rotating which part is held out. Metrics turn those held-out errors into numbers: MAE and RMSE for regression, accuracy, precision, recall and F1 for classification. You use them to choose a model, a threshold or a feature set before spending money on real deployment. The test set is a final exam, not a practice ground.
prereq: You need: linear regression, logistic regression and overfitting and bias-variance.

blocks.text: Generalisation error is the error on new cases. You cannot see it directly, so you hold data back. A hold-out split has three parts: train (fit weights), validation (choose hyperparameters, threshold or features) and test (report once). A single split is noisy: a lucky test set flatters the model.

items: Shuffle the cases and cut them into k equal folds; k = 5 or k = 10 is common.
For j = 1 to k: train on the other k−1 folds, score on fold j.
Average the k scores. Report the mean and the standard deviation.
Stratified k-fold keeps the positive-class fraction the same in every fold; use it when one class is rare.
Leave-one-out sets k = n: train on n−1 cases, test on one. It is slow for large n.
The test set is touched once, after all choices.

sections.h3: Regression metrics: MAE, MSE, RMSE and R²

blocks.text: Regression metrics measure the gap between actual yᵢ and prediction ŷᵢ for n cases; ȳ is the mean of the actual values.

blocks.where: MAE is mean absolute error; yᵢ is the actual target for case i; ŷᵢ is the predicted target; n is the number of cases. MAE is in the target's units.
MSE is mean squared error; each error is squared before averaging. Its unit is the square of the target unit.
RMSE is root mean squared error. It returns to target units and punishes large errors more than MAE.
R² is the fraction of variance explained; ȳ is the mean actual target. R² = 1 is perfect; R² = 0 means predicting ȳ; negative R² is worse than the mean.

blocks.text: Classification starts with a confusion matrix at one threshold: TP true positives, FP false positives, FN false negatives, TN true negatives. Some syllabi call this whole step model assessment.

blocks.where: Accuracy is the share of all cases classified correctly.

blocks.text: Precision = TP / (TP + FP); Recall = TP / (TP + FN); Specificity = TN / (TN + FP)
blocks.where: Precision asks: when the model says positive, how often is it right? Recall asks: of real positives, how many were found? Specificity is the true-negative rate.
F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. It balances the two.

blocks.text: ROC plots recall (true-positive rate) against 1−specificity (false-positive rate) as the threshold moves. AUC is the area under it: 0.5 is random, 1.0 is perfect. Class imbalance breaks accuracy. If 5% are fraud, a model that always says no fraud is 95% accurate and catches nothing. Use precision, recall, F1 or AUC, and stratified folds. For model selection, compare models by mean CV score on the same folds; prefer the simpler model when scores are close. Tune on validation folds, then test once. Domain shift warning: a model trained on old UPI fraud patterns can fail when fraud changes; recheck on fresh data.

figure.caption: Five-fold cross-validation on 200 cases: four folds fit the model, the fifth scores it, and the five scores are averaged. Notice that every case is tested exactly once.

spec.title: 5-fold cross-validation
spec.aria: Five-fold cross-validation splits 200 cases into five folds, trains on four, tests on one, and averages the five scores.

examples.question: A classifier is tested on 200 cases: TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 20, TN = 130. Compute accuracy, precision, recall, specificity and F1. Separately, five-fold CV accuracies are 0.80, 0.82, 0.78, 0.84, 0.81; compute the mean.
examples.answer: Accuracy 0.850, precision 0.80, recall 0.667, specificity 0.929, F1 0.727; mean CV accuracy 0.81.
examples.check:
tp = 40
fp = 10
fn = 20
tn = 130
acc = (tp + tn) / (tp + fp + fn + tn)
prec = tp / (tp + fp)
rec = tp / (tp + fn)
spec = tn / (tn + fp)
f1 = 2 * prec * rec / (prec + rec)
cv = [0.80, 0.82, 0.78, 0.84, 0.81]
mean_cv = sum(cv) / len(cv)
print(round(acc, 3))
print(round(prec, 3))
print(round(rec, 3))
print(round(spec, 3))
print(round(f1, 3))
print(round(mean_cv, 3))

traps: Tuning on the test set. The test set is scored once, after all choices; otherwise it becomes a validation set and your reported score is optimistic.
Reporting accuracy on imbalanced data. A 95% accurate classifier can miss every positive case when positives are rare.
Confusing precision and recall. Precision divides by predicted positives (TP + FP); recall divides by actual positives (TP + FN).
Forgetting units and scale. MSE is in squared target units; RMSE and MAE are in target units, so compare them with the target's range.
Data leakage in cross-validation. Scaling, imputing or selecting features before the fold split lets test information leak into training; fit those steps inside each fold.

quiz.a: Split the data into k folds; for each fold, train on the other k−1 folds and score on the held-out fold; average the k scores.

quiz.q: Why use stratified folds when positives are 5% of the data?
quiz.a: Plain random folds can put very few or no positives in a fold, so the score is unstable. Stratified folds keep the 5% positive share in every fold.

quiz.q: A test set has TP = 30, FP = 20, FN = 10, TN = 140. Compute precision, recall and F1.
Model A has five-fold accuracy 0.90 with SD 0.01; model B has 0.92 with SD 0.05 on the same folds. What should you check before choosing B?
quiz.a: Check fold-by-fold differences, whether B's gain is consistent, and the cost of errors. B's high SD means its mean may not generalise; prefer A if scores overlap and simplicity matters.

quiz.q: A regression model has SSE = 200 and SST = 800 on test data. Compute R².
Why is AUC useful when classes are imbalanced?
quiz.a: AUC measures ranking across all thresholds, not one accuracy cut. It does not reward a model that always predicts the majority class.

quiz.q: A fraud model scores AUC 0.95 on last year's UPI data but fails this year. Give one likely cause and one check.
quiz.a: Domain shift: fraud patterns changed. Recheck on fresh labelled data and compare recent precision, recall and AUC before deployment.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice, libraries such as scikit-learn provide cross_val_score, StratifiedKFold and precision_recall_curve, so you rarely write the loop by hand. Nested cross-validation separates tuning from scoring when you compare many models. Search next for nested cross-validation, calibration curves and precision-recall AUC.
